I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal items 'others can see what happened to me' and 'ashamed of what happened to my body' imply a trauma with visible bodily violation or injury, most classically interpersonal/sexual trauma, and are hard to reconcile with a generic man-made disaster trauma in the absence of any corroborating memory or trigger content about bodily injury or disfigurement.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Being Touched' is specifically linked to bodily violation/contact-based trauma and fits poorly with the rest of the profile for man-made disaster. The threat items center on environmental danger and escape planning, creating a cross-node mismatch with this touch-avoidance strategy.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: These items imply a trauma with prominent bodily violation or physical injury consequences. For a man-made disaster trauma, this specific body-focused pattern is not impossible, but in the absence of any supporting memory or trigger content and alongside the other items emphasizing generalized danger, it stands out as a hard-to-explain shift toward an assault/injury formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
issues.explanation: Within the current profile, avoidance of touch and bodily stress appears organized around bodily harm/shame, but the threat items are about environmental danger, escape planning, and unfamiliar places. That makes the strategy set only partially connected to the expressed threat/appraisal pattern.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: The profile is otherwise centered on persistent danger, vigilance, scanning, escape planning, and avoidance of unfamiliar places, which coheres with threat-focused beliefs after a man-made disaster. 'Failed Role' introduces a distinct self-evaluative theme that is not supported by the rest of the selected items and is hard to reconcile with this otherwise purely danger/safety formulation. Given the active formulation emphasizes Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies and Maladaptive Strategies → Threat, a danger-based appraisal would better fit the linked hypervigilance and checking strategies than a role-failure appraisal.

vignette:
Priya, a 32-year-old city council member, presented as poised and articulate, yet her hands were clenched so tightly in her lap they were drained of color. She had built her career on being a visible, accessible public servant, but for the past eight months, she confessed, leaving her apartment felt like preparing for battle. The shift began the night of the community center annex collapse. She had been at the podium, fielding questions about a new zoning ordinance, when the first groan of stressed metal echoed through the hall. She remembered the ceiling seeming to ripple, the shower of dust, and then a deafening roar as the back third of the building gave way. She was uninjured, but the memory of the chaos, the screams, and the sight of twisted rebar where a fire exit used to be was inescapable.

In the weeks that followed, a pervasive sense of dread began to colonize her life. The world, which had once felt knowable and largely safe, now seemed riddled with invisible fractures. This profound feeling of imminent threat began to calcify into a set of rigid beliefs. Sleep offered little respite, as she found it harder to feel safe at night, lying awake listening for any sound that was out of place. Her apartment, once a sanctuary, now felt like a fragile container she had to constantly monitor. This nightly state of high alert reinforced a grim new philosophy: the world was, in fact, a fundamentally dangerous place. She was certain that the collapse wasn't a freak accident but a confirmation of a hidden, terrible truth. She had come to believe that she had to be on guard all the time, because you never knew what could happen next.

This conviction that constant vigilance was the only rational response to an inherently unsafe world began to dictate her every action. Her work, which demanded public engagement, became a minefield. Before entering any room—the council chambers, a constituent’s office, a coffee shop—she would first identify all possible escape routes, her mind tracing the path from her chair to the door. During meetings, she found herself unable to focus on agendas or debates; instead, she was constantly scanning her surroundings, her eyes sweeping over the crowd, assessing each face for any sign of malice, any hint of a threat. She became hypervigilant for anyone who seemed agitated or out of place, her body tensing whenever someone approached her unexpectedly. She started declining invitations to ribbon-cuttings and town halls held in unfamiliar venues, telling her staff she had scheduling conflicts when, in truth, the thought of being in a new place where she couldn't assess the danger was paralyzing.

These strategies, meant to keep her safe, have instead drawn the walls of her world in tighter, creating a feedback loop of fear. The more she scans her environment for threats, the more she finds: a loud bang from the street, a crack in the plaster, a disgruntled citizen in the gallery. Each observation serves as fresh evidence, sharpening her sense of being in constant peril. The very act of avoiding unfamiliar places has made the familiar world feel smaller and the unknown world outside it monstrously threatening. Her hypervigilance has taken a professional toll; colleagues have commented on her being distracted and jumpy, and she feels a growing distance from the very constituents she entered public service to help. They are no longer people to connect with, but potential dangers to be managed.

Priya finally sought therapy after an incident last week. She was scheduled to speak at the opening of a new library branch, an event she had championed for years. But standing outside the gleaming glass-and-steel building, all she could see were potential points of failure. The weight of the structure, the stress on the windows, the sheer number of people inside—it was too much. She fled back to her car, overwhelmed by a physical sense of dread, and missed the event entirely. She is terrified that this fear will not only cost her the career she loves but will one day leave her unable to leave her home at all. Her hope is simple, yet feels impossibly distant: to once again stand at a podium and feel the floor beneath her feet as solid ground.
